speechtext:
I should like to make a few observations in regard to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) in the bill now before the house. In the first place I wish it to be understood that I have a good deal of sympathy for the object the hon. member has in view, that is, the reduction of the differential between export rates and domestic rates as far as western grain and flour are concerned, but I submit that this bill will not achieve the purpose he has in mind. I believe it will make matters a good deal worse than they are at present; it will make confusion worse confounded, if I have correctly interpreted the sections of the act which it is proposed to amend.
This bill contains two sections only. It is proposed to amend section 320 of the Railway Act by striking out the words "in the interests of the public," and inserting in lieu thereof the words "national interest, both producing and consuming." I find that the words "in the interests of the public" have been in the Railway Act since 1919, when the act was first introduced in the house, and since then certain practices have grown up with reference to the interpretation of those words. I have before me a memorandum of the Board of Railway Commissioners defining the interpretation which has been placed on those words by the board, and before proceeding I should like to read that definition:
The present wording, by judicial construction, has come to mean "the public of -the locality or district affected, and that any considerable portion of the population in general as opposed to an individual, or association of individuals, will satisfy the description"; "the controlling power or effective competition on particular rates"; "the legitimate desire of the railway company to secure the traffic is not only to be considered, but also whether it is in the interests of the public that -they should secure it, or abandon it, or not attempt to secure it. One class of cases intended to be covered is where traffic from a distance is charged low rates, because unless such low rates are charged it will not come into the market at all"; "the fact that a trader has access to a competing
IMr. Gordon.]

Railway Act
route for the carriage of his goods may be taken into consideration by the board in deciding whether lower tolls, or rates, charged to such trader constitutes an undue preference."
I must say that it is difficult for me to understand just what is meant by the proposed amendment. I submit that the change may have a more restricted application than the present wording. In addition I wish to point out that under section 320 the tolls referred to are not tolls prescribed by the Board of Railway Commissioners but tolls initiated by the railway companies under the provisions of sections 331 and 332 of the act, which my hon. friend might peruse if he is not familiar with them. Section 328 states:
The tariffs of tolls which the company shall be authoribed to issue under this act for the carriage of goods between points on the railway shall be divided into three classes,
(a)	the standard freight tariff;
(b)	special freight tariffs; and
(c)	competitive tariffs.
Those are the tariffs which the railway companies may initiate in order to attract business to their systems; they are not tolls which have been prescribed by the raiway board. Where tolls are prescribed or directed by the board, full consideration is given to the avoidance of unjust discrimination or undue preference ; that is a prerequisite to their direction. They must be fully considered from every angle, not only from the point of view of the railway companies themselves but also from that of the shippers, the consumers and the producing public.
The hon. gentleman also proposes to add subsection (2) to section 320, as follows:
The board may consider the question of what should be reasonable compensation under the circumstances, and may establish a rate structure in the interests of trade development and public policy, though such experimental rates may not at the time or of themselves give reasonable compensation to the railway companies.
I understand that the hon. member has two objactives in view; first, that the board may consider the question of what shall be reasonable compensation under the circumstances, and second, that the board may establish a rate structure in the interests of trade development and public policy, though such experimental rates may not at the time or of themselves give reasonable compensation to the railway companies. I submit that the meaning of the first part of this amendment is not very clear. It can hardly relate to subsection 1 of this section, because if the board found as a fact that a lower toll was necessary for the purpose of securing traffic, then obviously such lower toll would be reasonable
compensation under the circumstances. Therefore I fail to see how it can refer to the first part of this section. Nor does it seem to relate to the latter part, because if the board established a rate structure in the interests of trade development and public policy, though such rates might not at the time or of themselves give reasonable compensation, what would be the object of the board at the same time giving consideration to what would be reasonable compensation? There would be no object in it at all, as far as I can see.
With regard to the second point, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) has already declared that at the present time the government cannot accept that suggestion. As I understand the declaration of the minister, parliament is the proper place to decide matters of that kind. Just here I might add that if hon. members will look up the freight rate discussion of 1925 they will find that on all sides of the house it was admitted that the proper tribunal to deal with such a complicated question as the freight rate structure of this country was the railway board, and not parliament. It is also difficult to determine how far a rate structure of the character described should be carried. If hon. gentlemen will recall the discussion which took place in this house a short time ago in connection with western freight rates they will remember that certain commodities were referred to as coming within this definition. To any of these commodities might be applied the amendment which my hon. friend offers for the improvement of the situation in British Columbia: gasoline; products of British Columbia moving into the prairies; cordwood, and domestic rates generally in Quebec; live stock; potatoes and hay. It is also conceivable that the rates on coal from Alberta and the maritimes moving to central Canada would come in for consideration under the proposed amendment. You can therefore see the far-reaching effect which the hon. gentleman's amendment would have.
The Board of Railway Commissioners, under the general supervision of the Railway Act, to which no amendment is proposed, must fix and determine rates which will be just and reasonable, and this means reasonable not only for the railways but as well to shippers, producers, consumers and all classes in the dominion. If the board established experimental rates which would, on the traffic concerned, give reasonable compensation to the railway companies, should the board then arbitrarily impose an increase in rates on some of the traffic of the railways to make up the loss of revenue to the railways in consequence
Railway Act

of such experimental rates? Would this be practicable or reasonable? Would it be reasonable to shift the compensation of the railways from one commodity to another, and would it improve the situation in the long run, even supposing such changes were made? Moreover, I submit that it would subject the railways to serious losses of revenue.
With respect to the proposed amendment to subsection 5 of section 325 to provide statutory rates on grain and flour moving from the prairie provinces to Pacific points, the present rates are prescribed and approved by the board. This matter has been adjudicated. We have had it under discussion before and we know that the rates at present in force are those which have been submitted to the board, fully examined and carefully inquired into, and they are rates which the board have considered fair and reasonable to all parties. Should this amendment be carried, the differential between the export and domestic rates might be lessened but it might lead to an increase in the export rate, or it might make the domestic rate and the export rate the same. In addition to that, it would result in a reduction in the present export rates to Vancouver, published by the Canadian Pacific Railway, which in turn would necessarily reduce the rates of the Canadian National Railways. I would refer my hon. friend to the board's judgment in the general freight rates investigation, volume 17 of the board's judgments and orders, for full information in this regard. There the hon. gentleman will find the judgment of the board given with respect to the western freight rates question.
The proposed amendment, I submit, would result in heavy reductions in the earnings of both the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways. Rates therein provided from prairie points to Pacific coast points should apply on and after June 27, 1925. It is difficult to determine by just what amount the revenues of the two railways might be reduced if the amendment were to go into effect, but I am given to understand that so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned, it might lead to a reduction in revenue of $500,000 per annum. As this amendment is supposed to be retroactive to the 27th of June, 1925, that would mean that the Canadian National Railways would have to refund some $3,500,000, and I am certainly of the opinion that the Canadian Pacific Railway would have to refund a much greater sum; so that in connection with these two railways it would amount to $8,000,000 or $10,000,000. I submit that at a time like this, when all railways are suffering from declining 
revenues, and when their revenues are still on the downgrade, this is a very inopportune moment for my hon. friend to offer an amendment such as this. There is some reason in the argument he advances that the differential between the export and import rates should be reduced, but I submit in all earnestness that this is neither the time nor the proper method of applying the remedy he seeks. I shall have to vote against the proposed bill.

speechtext:
Regarding the first two proposals in the bill, I may say briefly, in reply to my hon. friend from Cariboo, that these two were incorporated in it in view of the report of the Duncan commission. If I read from the report I think the point will be explained more fully and clearly than possibly I could state it myself:
At present the work of the railway commission is circumscribed within the two considerations, viz:-
(a)	Reasonable compensation to the carrying company, and
(b)	No unfair preference or unjust discrimination as between traders.
Section 320 of the Railway Act seems to give the wider powers that we have in mind to the railway commission, so far as the question of undue preference or unjust discrimination may be involved:-
"320. In deciding whether a lower tell, or difference in treatment, does or does not amount to an undue preference or an unjust discrimination, the board may consider whether such lower toll, or difference in treatment is necessary for the purpose of securing, in the interests of the public the traffic in respect of which it is made, and whether such object cannot be attained without unduly reducing the higher toll."
That is how the act reads at present, and the Duncan commission, referring thereto, say:
Even there we feel that, if the intention was to have larger national interests in rnind, the section should be made clearer, and instead of the words "in the interests of the public"

(which might be interpreted as in the interests of the 'consuming' public), the words should clearly state that it is national interests (both 'producing' and 'consuming') that are in mind. If this was not the original intention of the section, we suggest it is the intention which should now be imported into it. We feel further that a similar extension of authority should be imparted to the railway board in regard to the question of reasonable compensation. It would then be competent for the railway board to make a survey of just the very character that the president of the Canadian National Railways testified as being part of his function (as the business head of a railway); and if from public policy they felt that an experimental rate should be conceded, they should be free to constitute the rate, even although it might not, at the time, or of itself, give reasonable compensation to the railway company.
It was with that end in view that I had the bill so drafted as to give to the Board of Railway Commissioners, as suggested here, these powers which I think it very desirable that they should have. I do not intend to go again into the various phases of the act; that is scarcely necessary because it has been explained many times.
Now, I am not making an appeal on sympathetic grounds. With the exception of a few years, the Crowsnest pass agreement had been in effect until 1925, when it was amended This was brought about by a decision of the supreme court which ruled that the Crowsnest rate applied only to the points in existence when the agreement was made and only within the territory which was then within the scope of the agreement of 1897. It is just ns well to remember that the Crowsnest rate was intended to give the prairies protection on freight, and especially grain, as there was no water competition as existed in eastern portions of Canada. The decision of the supreme court would have brought about a chaotic condition in railway rates which would have resulted in one station getting the Crowsnest rate while the next station would get some other rate, and in order to overcome this difficulty the government of the day in 1925, introduced the amendments which are now a part of the Railway Act. The amendments of 1925 gave to all towns on the prairies the benefit of the Crowsnest rates on grain and flour, but they took away the Crowsnest commodity rates which had been in effect from points included in the 1897 agreement. At the time the amendments were under discussion the information was given that the prairie provinces were gaining as well as losing something, but it must be remembered that the railways gained something through the wiping out of the Crowsnest rates on commodities.
Railway Act
British Columbia did not come under the provisions of the new amendments, as I contend it should have. Grain does not change to something else simply because it goes west instead of east. At that time it was thought that the Board of Railway Commissioners would have the power to adjust rates and prevent discrimination, but we have since learned to our sorrow and loss that such is not the case. The decision of the supreme court and decisions of the board itself have since demonstrated clearly that the board has not the power to do this.
The interest of the prairie provinces is identical with the interest of British Columbia. It is to their interest that grain should go west as cheaply as it does east, especially as British Columbia is providing a market for the cheaper grades of wheat. One of the chief reasons which prompted me to introduce this bill, the result of a long study of the whole matter, is the realization that British Columbia, in my opinion, will never obtain a reduction in the freight rates on grain and flour by an appeal to the Board of Railway Commissioners. The decision of the supreme court precludes the possibility of using the Crowsnest pass rates to Fort William as a basis for argument. It seems to me that we in British Columbia are simply wasting our time, energy and money by appealing to the board, and it is time this parliament recognized that fact. According to the ruling of the board, the Crowsnest rates on grain and flour going east to Fort William are no argument as to discrimination and cannot be used as an argument for discrimination because of the decision given by the supreme court. Canadian Pacific Railway officials have also sworn that no one can tell the exact cost of hauling any one commodity.
Another important fact to be remembered is that grain is just grain when going to Fort William, but when going west it becomes either domestic grain or export grain. The domestic rate to British Columbia is higher than the export rate-almost twice as high-and this is against all railway precedents. The cheaper and inferior article shipped to our province is paying a higher freight rate than the better quality of grain which is exported.
I am somewhat disappointed in the attitude taken by the house, and I am especially disappointed in the attitude taken by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber). The hon. member rose in his place the other evening and said he could not support this measure because in the first place the bill was not before him. As a matter of fact the
Railway Act

bill was introduced on April 12; it was called for first reading on April 15 and had come up for second reading on April 22 when the hon. member spoke and said he had not the bill before him. What is in the bill that requires such a lot of interpretation? The second clause is so simple that any backwoods man could understand its meaning. It reads in part:
-and to all such traffic moving westwardly from Fort William and from aill points on all lines of railway west of Fort William, to Vancouver, British Columbia and to ports on the Pacific coast.
Surely it would not take a great deal of time to discover that all we are asking for is the same freight rates to British Columbia on domestic grain as are paid by the people in the east on grain from the prairie provinces to Fort William, Quebec, Montreal or Nova Scotia.
I repeat that I am disappointed in the attitude taken by hon. members, especially those from British Columbia. I can recall their advocating such a measure in the past, but it seems that when the test comes they do not feel like coming through. The hon. member for Fraser Valley comes from a poultry district, and he knows that the people in British Columbia have been clamouring for this relief for years. Perhaps he was too busy delving back to the year 1925 to find out what was said in those days, but I am more interested in the conditions applying to-day and which will apply in the future. I introduced this bill because I believed that this was the time to show that we really wanted what we were asking for. Because of the decision of the supreme court I do not believe that British Columbia will be able to get any satisfaction from the Board of Railway Commissioners. I commend the bill to the house.

subtopic: AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING MEASURES TO RELIEVE DISTRESS
speechtext:
On my way up to the house I saw a fairly large truck on which was a sign "Daily Service." It reminded me of what my good friend the Minister of Railways said in the house not long ago about the unfair competition of trucks with the railways. His speech on that occasion made a great impression on me. Let me sum up the whole matter in this way: if the trans-Canada highway brings returns, they will be due to unfair competition with the railways. On the other hand, if it produce no returns, the expenditure on it will be an utter waste. This is the dilemma (that confronts us at present.
We must also consider the maintenance of the road after its completion. Several million dollars might be invested in the scheme and the expenditure on maintenance would be very heavy. Let us count the number of British Columbia automobiles that visit Nova Scotia and the number from Nova Scotia which one might see in British Columbia. They are very few. Some, however, are coming by way of the border states and they might be counted on the Detroit bridge, for instance, but many of the cars coming from the west or from the east and crossing that bridge do not go as far as the ocean.
I am strongly against any kind of hybrid legislation, such as is half federal and half provincial. The expenditure of money should be made by either the .provinces or the federal government; if the provinces require additional sums to meet their expenditures, such sums should be given by the federal govern-
2614	COMMONS
Unemployment-Agreements with Provinces
ment, not earmarked for roads or schools or any particular purpose but by way of an increase in the provincial subsidy in order that every province should have full control of the money handed to it. According to the British North America Aot each province has full jurisdiction within its borders, while the federal government has jurisdiction only when a matter affects two or more .provinces. That principle of law is well known noit only to every lawyer but to any man who has made some study of constitutional matters. If we have a trans-Canada highway in which the federal government is interested, it should be built by the federal government alone. But, on the other hand, if the federal government is not interested, then each province should build its own share of the highway. At the present time most of the provinces have their own road policy, and I believe that each province should have complete control of its roads. I do not see how the federal government can give money to the provinces for the building of roads. If the provinces require money for some purpose or other and the provincial subsidy is not enough, the federal government should come to the rescue of the province and increase the subsidy, and if the subsidy of one province is increased, the subsidy of all provinces should be increased in proportion. May I ask the minister to be kind enough to let me know if he will consider the suggestion that I made this afternoon with regard to a complete inventory of the unemployed?

subtopic: AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING MEASURES TO RELIEVE DISTRESS
speechtext:
The attacks made by my hon. friend from Temiseouata on the transjCanada highway, and particularly that section in the district from which I come were of such a character that I feel they cannot be allowed to pass without some remarks from a representative of that part of the country.
In the first place I would say that no contribution could be made by the dominion and the provinces of Canada that would tend to so great an extent to knit all the provinces together and to develop the whole country as a contribution to the trans-Canada highway. It will be a means by which the citizens of Prince Edward Island in the east can motor across Canada on Canadian soil all the way to the west coast, and vice versa.
Frankly I was amazed at the parochialism of my hon. friend in his references not only to the trans-Canada highway but also to a part of this country .about 'which he apparently knows nothing whatever. If his remarks had not been made in the House of Commons one would not have paid any attention to them, 
but going out to the people of this country and to the world outside of Canada as uttered by a member of the House of Commons, they are deserving of some consideration.
With reference to that section of the trans-Canada highway where a very considerable amount of construction work will be necessary to build the road, that is that section in northern Ontario, that part of Canada lying between the Ottawa river and the boundary line of Manitoba, the manifest lack of knowledge of that country that my hon. friend discloses is such that one can scarcely imagine a man in public life anywhere would go out of his way to the extent my hon. friend has done to belittle a part of Canada in which you could lose the settled portions of Ontario and of Quebec combined. Lying north of the height of land in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, in my hon. friend's province and in the province in which I happen to live, there is more arable land than is now under cultivation in the whole of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. There are today more farmers in the district of Nipissing, represented by my hon. friend from Sudbury (Mr. Hurtubise) than there, are in the county of Temiseouata. There are more farmers in South Timiskaming, represented by the hon. Minister of Labour, than there are in the county of Temiseouata. There are more farmers in East Algoma or in West Algoma than there are in the county of Temiseouata, and these farmers, many of them, are of my hon. friend's own race, a happy, contented people, helping to develop this country. Ultimately the tens of thousands of farmers who will yet go into that country will make it a greater farming area than the settled portions of Quebec and Ontario combined.
It is true that there are rocks in northern Ontario; it is true that there are lakes in northern Ontario; it is true that there are mines in northern Ontario. But I would point out to my hon. friend that northern Ontario produced more new wealth in the past ten years than all the rest of the province of Ontario, to say nothing of the province of Quebec-new wealth in the form of minerals, agricultural produce, timber, pulp and paper, and the baser metals.
With regard to the work that has been done on the trans-Canada highway, my hon. friend referred to the fact that there had been blasting of rocks on the north shore of lake Superior. It might surprise my hon. friend to know that there has not been one dollar spent on the north shore of lake Superior. Where blasting ivas done was on the stretch

Unemployment-Agreements with Provinces
of road between Nipigon, fifty or sixty miles east of Port Arthur, and the boundary line of Manitoba. I would suggest to my hon. friend that he consult his colleague, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, as to the character of the country through which that portion of the highway runs, and ascertain from him if it is a barren wilderness or desert such as he pictured to the house this afternoon. I have travelled across Canada from coast to coast. I have gone around the south shore of the St. Lawrence river by rail and by water. I have seen its little fishing villages nestling up against the rocky shores, and the patches of arable land sprinkled about. It is delightful country with great scenic attractions for the tourist, and simply because it is small in area as compared with that vast extent of fourteen hundred miles running almost from the city of Ottawa to the city of Winnipeg, one does not attempt to belittle it or suggest that it is a wilderness or a scene of utter desolation or a useless and worthless country. It is nothing of the kind. Everyone admires its beauty.
As to the influence of the trans-Canada highway on the traffic of the transcontinental railways, I would suggest that my hon. friend discuss this subject with someone who understands the principles of transportation, with Sir Henry Thornton, president of the Canadian National Railways, if you like; and he will tell you at once that it is not the traffic that goes on a highway of that character that is taking away revenue from the railways. The tourist traffic that is brought into the country and that will be brought into it by means of highways of the kind we are now discussing will furnish more traffic to the railways than any possible loss they can experience by reason of such a highway being built. The live stock of the west will never be brought east in trucks, and merchandise will never be taken from the east to the west in trucks. Mr. Chairman, in the course of the discussion the question of putting men on the land has been considered. Hon. members are not yet very clear as to the attitude of the government. On a former occasion the minister seemed to indicate that the government did not intend to cooperate with the provinces or to enter upon any scheme themselves of putting men back upon the land. More recently it would seem that the government at least in some degree has changed its mind, and that there is a possibility of some such work being undertaken. If such a policy is in contemplation it ought to be undertaken with the greatest care. Any attempt to enter upon anything as elaborate as the soldier settlement scheme would from the beginning be doomed to failure.
Much has been said about putting men back on the land, by people who evidently know very little about conditions confronting those actually on the land. Many statements have been made which would not for one moment bear investigation, and indicate an entire lack of information. For instance, we heard the statement a few days ago that the farmer would at least have his butter and eggs. The hon. member was evidently under the impression that butter and eggs could be picked off trees. The minister has given the figure of $600 as a sum which might possibly be advanced to men desiring to take up farming. I would say that $600 would be only a flea bite when compared with what is neces-
sarv properly to establish a man on a farm in the west. True, there is a possibility that if a very careful selection were made of the men to go on the land something might be done in establishing some of them on bush farms in northern Ontario. If those men were willing to face many years of privation and hardship as did our forefathers in Ontario and Quebec seventy-five or one hundred years ago, there would be some possibility of their making a reasonable success. Unfortunately, however, to-day there are very few men possessed of the temperament and the willingness to face years of pioneering in the woods. In any policy which may be advocated to plac'e men back upon the land, that fact must be taken into consideration. I do not say that something could not be done in that direction, but I wish to emphasize that any policy along that line must be undertaken with great care, and that any elaborate policy would from the outset be doomed to failure.
I noticed that the International Harvester Company of Chicago, using road tractors and ploughs, were ploughing up a large area of land around the city of Chicago, with a view to dividing it into quarter-acre lots to be cultivated by the unemployed. In war time some such scheme was undertaken in and around the city of Winnipeg; men were encouraged to cultivate garden lots. Unfortunately, however, the time is rapidly approaching when such a scheme would be impracticable for this year, because the seed would have to be in the ground within the next month. That policy might have met with a large degree of success. Men and women living in Winnipeg or in any of the cities of eastern Canada could have been given an opportunity to cultivate some of the adjoining vacant lots. But the time for such a program is almost if not completely passed.
It seems perfectly evident from all the information we can gather that we are rapidly approaching the time when to a very much greater extent than in the past we will be required to give direct relief. Certainly it is true that the provinces and the municipalities cannot longer cooperate with the federal government as they have done in carrying on relief works. The municipalities in particular are at the point where, not being able to collect their taxes, they will not be able to contribute further money to the carrying on of works not absolutely and immediately needed. But facing, as I think we are compelled to face, this question of giving direct relief, I want to bring to the notice of the house a matter that has been of interest to me for some months past.

Unemployment-Agteements with Provinces
Hon. members may be aware of the fact that, in the United States, of the 200,000,000 bushels of farm board wheat they have had in storage for some time past the government have contributed 40,000,000 bushels for the direct relief of the unemployed. I have had particular reasons for being interested in that proposition, and I may tell the house that the proposal which passed congress early in March is now being carried into effect in many United States cities. The movement began in this way:	One of the professors of Oberlin
college conceived the idea that through the use of wheat ground by the primitive methods which prevailed in pioneer days much might be done to feed the unemployed. In regard to the people of the United States I might say this:	They do not seem to have done as
much by way of federal governmental relief as we have done in Canada. The burden has been thrown more upon the state governments, the municipalities and private charity. The situation confronting them now is that they have reached the bottom of their community chests.
As I say, this scheme was inaugurated by one who had interested himself in the question, and he was able to show that by taking the available wheat and having it ground in this primitive way it would be possible to provide meals for the unemployed at a cost of three cents each. This demonstration was carried out in the city of Lorain, Ohio. I visited that section of the country during the Easter holidays, and in that city, which is an industrial centre with a large number of unemployed, by the use of two old fashioned pepper mills and a second hand farm feed mill, they were grinding flour and giving it out to the people. I saw the flour; I ate pancakes, waffles, muffins and even cookies made from that flour, and it was all that could be desired. The authorities were somewhat slow in adopting that proposition, but finally the Red Cross became interested in it, and all over the United States they are now making use of this farm board wheat ground in the primitive and simple way. While I was there at Easter the first carload of that wheat reached the town of Lorain, and since then I have received word to the effect that all that wheat has been used up, and they are asking for more. While I was there those who had originated the scheme visited the city of Cleveland, and the mayor of that city stated that by this plan they would be able to effect a saving to the community chest of $400,000 in the following three months.
I bring this to the attention of the house and the country because it does seem to me 41761-165
that if we are to be faeed* as we will be faced, with the problem of giving more direct relief to those who are in need, through some such means as this we might do a very great deal to give the people food that Will be perfectly wholesome and that will help them over the time of their unemployment. Seeing as I did what was being done by the means I have indicated, I have no hesitation in saying that if our churches, our philanthropic societies and our Red Cross, in cooperation with government institutions, would adopt such a scheme as this, we would be able to meet the need, which I am afraid will be facing us much more seriously than in the past, in a way that would afford great relief to the unemployed.
If any person cares to see it I have here a copy of an address given by the gentleman who originated the scheme, in which he outlines all the steps from the time they attempted to impress its merits on the people of the different communities, right up to the time it received the sanction of the United States government. I would not think it fitting to put this address on the records of the house, but if any hon. member or any charitably disposed people such as the Red Cross or any other philanthropic society would like further information with regard to what is being done in that direction I shall be very happy to give it.

The resolution before the chair reads in part:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to authorize the governor in council to enter into agreements ... to assist in defraying the cost of the sale and distribution of products of field, farm, sea, river and mine.
I suggest that the word "forest" should be included. I do not think there is any industry in Canada to-day that has been and is suffering more than the lumbering industry, and according to this resolution as it stands at present there is no relief in sight. I sincerely hope that when the bill comes before the house the word "forest" will be included. The lumbering industry has suffered for a number of years. It is in a peculiar situation; its product ordinarily does not go on the market 41761-165J
until at least twenty-four months after operations have commenced. Many of the limits have been bought at very high prices, the ground rents are high, and those engaged in the industry from the Atlantic to the Pacific are in a very unenviable position. In this regard I would direct the attention of the government to the building trade of Canada, which is one of the greatest industries in this country. It distributes more money among the various trades and labour organizations than any other trade in Canada. In 1929 the building operations in the cities of Canada were valued at S234,944,549. This outlay was divided among the lumbermen from the forest to the planing mill, the stone quarries, the brick manufacturers, the cement manufacturers, the hardware manufacturers, the plumbers, the painters, the builders, the decorators and so on right through the whole field. In practically all these cases ninety per cent of the outlay is for labour. Ninety per cent of the cost of lumbering is labour, ninety per cent of the cost of producing brick is labour, and the same holds true through the various building industries.
For various reasons, this industry has fallen off tremendously. I hold in my hand a quotation from an American paper of recent date which states that the industry has dropped 60 per cent as compared with the same month of last year, and 85 per cent as compared with the same month in 1929.

I think employment for our people is the greatest problem facing Canada to-day, and I regret the resolution as brought down and the statement of the minister give us very little hope of any further employment being provided. Apparently the action of the government is to be practically limited to giving unemployment relief, in other words, to adopting the dole system, which I do not like. This problem of employment must be tackled vigorously. We must do something different from what has been done so far. I am sure anyone who will visit the different parks in Ottawa and other places where the unemployed men congregate will agree wth that old saying "Unemployment with money is leisure, but unemployment without money is hell." I have talked with quite a number of returned men who say that the life they are living to-day, unable to secure employment, is far worse than the life they led in the trenches. Years ago Sherman, the famous United States general said: "War is hell," and war is even worse to-day than it was then. When numbers of these Canadian returned men have travelled from one end of the country to the other and back looking for work, without being able to find enough to keep body and soul together, we cannot wonder that their position to-day is in their opinion much worse than it was when they were fighting in France.
I look upon unemployment as a disease which must result from one or two causes, either overproduction or underconsumption. If it results from overproduction, we should endeavour to divide up the work, shorten the
hours of labour. But I do not think it results from overproduction; I think our troubles result from underconsumption. I would admit at once that we can produce more than enough in the way of foodstuffs. The size of the human stomach is limited, and when you fill a man with food, there is no use in placing more before him. But the capacity of our people to enjoy goods and services, so far as we can see to-day, is practically unlimited. Unemployment, whether due to underconsumption or overproduction, is a man-made problem and capable of solution. We should devote ourselves to a solution of it rather than adopt mere palliatives such as are suggested in the resolution under consideration. Unemployment as it now exists can and must be cured. If it cannot be cured under the present system where production is for private profit, then we must have a change of system. I do not say that it is impossible for it to be cured under the present system, and I should like to see the house and the government try to cure it. To-day we are not making any attempt to solve the problem of unemployment.
Before I leave the question of overproduction, may I say that even in Canada we have, underconsumption in the matter of foodstuffs. I remember reading in the New Outlook, a paper published in Toronto by the United Church, I think in the issue of last January, that a doctor from Regina said there were hundreds, perhaps thousands of teen-age boys' in Saskatchewan going to bed hungry every night. We know that fruit rots in the orchards every year although there are thousands who who never get a taste of fruit of any kind. I have under my hand a little quotation taken from the New Republic. It is true that this refers to conditions in the United States, but conditions in some parts of Canada may be similar. It says:
In Detroit alone, it has been estimated by medical authorities, at least one person starves to death in every seven hours and fifteen minutes. A physician at the Receiving Hospital in this city reported recently that four people a day, on the average, are brought to the hospital too far gone from starvation for their lives to be saved. Many others die lonely deaths outside the hospitals. On one day in September, in Grand Circus park where the homeless gather, three workers were found dead.
It says :
Thousands of children are under-nourished; that a great number of suicides are not reported in the press; that the psychopathic wards of the hospitals are crowded with people whose minds have become unstrung under the pressure of adversity.

I pause here to say that I think the government of Canada has done better in regard to unemployment relief than the United States government; I give our government credit for that. We have made a fair attempt to hand out unemployment relief, but too much of the burden has been placed upon the provinces and municipalities, and many of the municipalities are practically bankrupt so that a different system of financing must be adopted this year. I remember reading last year that thousands die of starvation in China every year and that millions of Chinese go to bed hungry every night. If we could work out a proper system of distribution in this world, I cannot help feeling we would find there was no over-production even of wheat. When it comes to a question of overproduction of other commodities, I should like to quote for the benefit of the committee from Mr. Harvey Firestone, one of the most prominent business men in the United States. He says positively that our trouble is due to underconsumption, not overproduction. He says that in the United States there are four million city homes with no bath tub, three million city homes with no plumbing, four million rural homes with no electricity, thirteen million homes, both rural and urban, with no telephones, five million homes lacking adequate clothing, food and shelter, seven million homes with no automobile, twenty million families with not even a good radio.
I think we must agree with Mr. Firestone that the difficulty is due to underconsumption. Why cannot the copper which is going begging on commodity markets to-day be used to provide these people with telephones, radios and electrical service? By the way, it is rather significant the way they do things in the United States, and I suppose we do the same in Canada. I am told that in that country there is one automobile to every five people and one bath tub to every twenty people. It is quite easy to imagine five people riding in one automobile, but imagine twenty people taking a bath in one bath tub! There is plenty of potential demand in Canada and the United States for these things which the unemployed to-day would like to be making. The trouble is that there seems to be a great gap between production and consumption. The cause of underconsumption to-day is lack of money in the hands of those who would purchase these goods if they could. The old law of supply and demand, which has been much overworked, cannot operate to-day. There is potential demand, but it cannot become effective demand because the people 
have not the money in their pockets. We need a new money system. I believe that the want of a proper standard of purchasing power is the chief cause of the survival of the monstrous fallacy that there can be too much produced of anything.
If we are going to solve the question of unemployment and put our people to work we must have a different financial system. President Hoover says:
Credit is the bloodstream of our economic life. Restriction and destruction of credit cripples the revival and expansion of agriculture, industry, commerce and employment. . . . To-day business is bad because of lack of purchasing power among consumers.
R. S. Noble, of the Royal Bank of Canada, said last year that the depression was caused by a thoroughly stupid bank policy, and that France and the United States were the principal villains in the piece.
Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, now Senator Meighen, said last year in Toronto, and I am always glad to quote him in this house, because I think he is one of the ablest members that ever sat in this chamber:
If those who have too much wheat can exchange that wheat with those who have too much of something else, oil, gasoline, clothing: if people are in a position to do that, the world can use all the wheat there is to-day and more, all the oil, all the clothing and more. If people were in a position to exchange what they have too much of for what somebody else has too much of, we would see that there is not too much of anything. The trouble is that they are not in a position so to exchange. Were the facilities of exchange adequate, were the world's monetary system adequate to demands for exchange, then the three per cent increase in the world's products from year to year would mean a three per cent elevation in the standard of living each year for the masses of mankind.
I think I have quoted enough authorities to show that the unemployment which exists to-day is due primarily to an inefficient financial system. In support of my contention that this depression is due to monetary causes I could quote Lord D'Abernon of England, Sir Basil Blackett, Sir Leo Chiozza Money, Sir Gustav Cassel, one of the most eminent economists in Europe, Dr. Hans Luther of the Reichsbanlc in Germany, and one of our own most prominent bankers, the late Mr. Neill. I would also like to quote to the house from a review of Maynard Keynes book-"A Treatise on Money." Trade and employment, as Mr. Keynes shows from forty different angles, depend on what men do to currency and credit. This review says:
The volume of exchanges tthat can be made on a given price-level with a given volume of money, at a given turnover, is absolutely fixed.

More exchanges require more money. Unless the money is forthcoming business falls off, men are thrown out of work, and the vicious spiral of deflation gets under way. Yet money is the only item in a list of items a mile along with which business has to deal, over the supply of which man has absolute and unlimited control.
If we could only convince this committee and this house and the government that the amount of money we might have is absolutely under our own control, we could get a good start out of this depression inside of a year. The cause of this depression is the lack of money in the hands of purchasers; the only way to get out of it is to put money into circulation, and yet when we come to discuss unemployment, we spend very little time on the question of money. It is rather significant that in to-day's press there appears the following despatch from Washington, D.C. It is headed, "United States house recommends putting four billion dollars of new notes into the market," and reads as follows:
Washington, D.C., May 2.-The House of Representatives to-day passed a bill "for restoring and maintaining the purchasing power of the dollar," and to secure that end recommended that the Federal Reserve Board use its power and resources to put into the market $4,000,000,000 in federal reserve notes, if need be, to raise the price level of commodities.
The bill would add an amendment to the Federal Reserve account as follows:
"It is hereby declared to be the policy of the United States that the average purchasing power of the dollar as ascertained by the department of labour in the wholesale commodity markets for the period 1921 to 1929 inclusive shall be restored and maintained by the control of the volume of credit and currency."
I would like to point out to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the committee that I think there is ample justification for the amendment to the budget which was moved from this corner of the house. It has now been declared by congress that it should be the policy of their central bank in the United States to issue enough money to raise commodity price levels to the average level between 1921 and 1929. I do not think that there is any other known way at present of raising commodity price levels. I do not like to think that Canada is going to lag behind the United States in this regard, and the policy I would like to urge upon the government at this time is that it should take steps to increase the amount of money in circulation in Canada to raise commodity price levels and make it possible to put our people to work and to put purchasing power into their hands. Do not let us wait until the United States has done it, and then drag along three months
behind them. Let us begin it now and get some benefit from it while the United States is putting this new money to work in the market. May I remind the members of the house again that this bill which has passed the United States congress recommends that the federal reserve board should use its resources to put four billion dollars of federal reserve notes into the market.
I would remind the house of the debate which took place here some time ago in regard to state aid for national health. The statement was made by the hon. member for East Calgary that the greatest cause of sickness is poverty, and if we do not do something to check this depression in Canada and to put our people to work and restore their purchasing power, we are going to strike a blow at the health of the Canadian people from which it will take many years to recover.
While I am on this subject I want to protest against the policy of all governments in Canada, federal, provincial and municipal, of discharging their civil servants. I just happen to have handed to me lately a despatch from a western paper which states that in that city eight firemen have been laid off, to effect a yearly saving of 815,000. I expect it will not be very long before these same firemen will have to receive direct relief from the city. What is the sense of discharging men from a city payroll at a time like this? Surely our cities would be wise to maintain their fire departments at full strength.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Parry Sound upon the statement he made in the committee to-night concerning the need of some stimulus to the construction industry in Canada. I have before me the latest edition of The Commerce of the Nation. This is the May number, and I think arrived only yesterday or to-day. At page 38 there are indices of Canadian business conditions. The basis for the figures is the monthly average from 1929 to 1924 taken at 100. The information is as follows:

It will be noted that building permits awarded in the month of March this year were only about 43 per cent of what they were a year ago.
I should like again to suggest to the government the advisability of providing some housing scheme in Canada. I know of no better way to put money into circulation. Perhaps before considering this matter in detail I should say that thousands of people in Canada have already lost their homes owing to the unemployment which has existed for the last two years. Others have lost their farms, and still others their savings. Many citizens have lost their jobs, and with them their hope, their health and their selfrespect. Many have committed suicide or died prematurely because of the worry of it all. I believe it is high time we really took some effective steps to put our people to work. It is useless to look for permanent alleviation of present conditions without important social and financial changes. There is no doubt that industry in Canada is capable of producing more goods than it did in 1928. Industry, however, has come to a standstill, and as a result men, women and children are suffering. Most of them suffer in hopeless silence, not because they do not want to work or do not know how to produce; not because materials are scarce or machinery lacking, but because of an inadequate, inefficient monetary system which demands from them a great sacrifice. The scarcity is purely artificial.
The situation to-day might very well be likened to that of a horse tethered to a tree standing in the midst of a luxurious pasture. The horse walks in one direction, thereby winding the tie rope around the tree. After a while he finds himself with his nose close to the tree, unable to reach the grass. In other words, he is starving. There is plenty of luxurious grass within a short distance, if he had sense enough to turn around and walk in the other direction. If he has not sense enough to do that he must starve. We in Canada are in the same position. We have not sense enough to make use of the machinery and raw materials in our country so that our people may be put to work to produce the goods they require. In my view our people have a moral right to demand from their representatives and their government an immediate examination of the fundamental weaknesses of the gold standard, to be followed by some permanent correction of that standard or the adoption of a new one. To my mind there is no doubt that we should adopt an entirely new financial policy. It 
seems to me at the present time we are carrying on a sort of hunger strike. Why should we not give those people employment? The Prime Minister is reported to have said in Montreal a year and a half ago that the first duty of the Canadian government would be to provide work for the Canadian people. With that I heartily agree, but we have neglected our duty. Of course we can do nothing until the government acts, and I hope it will not be long before it is persuaded to take action.
I should like to quote from the new book by Doctor Robert Eisler entitled This Money Maze. The preface is written by Sir Josiah Stamp, who recently delivered such a splendid address in this building and the foreword is written by Sir Thomas Barclay, one of the most prominent bankers in England. Doctor Eisler says:
Nothing but the borrowing and spending power of the community can start the wheels of industry whirling again after such a prolonged lethargy and continual fall in prices.
Under present conditions the best way to put the spending power of the community to work is by government action. I know of no other way in which it can be done. I think we are quite justified in asking the government to take action. I should like to remind the committee of the many promises made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign. He said:
I accept the challenge, and I say again I will call parliament together at the earliest possible moment to provide at once a remedy,

employment for all who can and will work.
There is no doubt we have several hundred thousand people in Canada to-day who would and could work if they had it to do. When Canada entered the war in 1914 we did not hesitate to use all the nation's credit. We financed our part of the war on our own credit-, and by similar methods we could finance this war against poverty and unemployment if we would make use of our national credit. We have plenty of it.
I suggest first that we institute a housing scheme along the lines I suggested a few weeks ago. I will not go into the details of the plan to-night, but I should like to draw attention to an article which appeared recently in The Prairie Lumberman concerning a federal home building loan, and pointing out the work which would be given if such a scheme were adopted. The article is as follows:
Work would immediately be provided for a great body of men now unemployed and additional employment would immediately be spread throughout many industries now cutting down on their staffs.

I was told to-day of a construction company in Canada which issued the statement that next month they would be forced to lay off two hundred men. The article continues:
Carpenters, masons, plasterers, painters, plumbers, electricians-all the better paid trades who in turn would circulate their wages, thus providing additional employment-would become actively employed. Thousands of men now unemployed could be engaged in common labour-these men are now very largely an absolute charge upon their respective communities.	.
Railroads would profit by greater freight movements, rail workers would benefit, lumber mills and other manufacturing plants would start to operate, every type of requirement for the inside of the house also would be bene-fitted. Demand for goods of every description would become rapidly widespread. Coal would be needed to heat these new homes, thus affecting favourably the Canadian mines and adding to the employment situation favourably in that direction. There is practically no end to the benefits which would accrue if such a necessary step were to be taken.
There was some talk of bolshevism and communism in this house this afternoon, so I would direct the attention of hon. members of the committee to this significant statement: Bolshevism is well fed only when we refuse to give good healthy "food" such as the opportunity .to own their own homes to otherwise well-meaning citizens. If you want to stop the spread of bolshevism start creating a nation of home-owners. It makes a mighty big difference to a person's attitude when he owns something and that something is his own home.
Some of these homes might be built in the cities, and certainly there is need for a great many in the country as well. Then I would suggest to the government that they embark on a large program of public works. I think we should begin a program this year entailing an ultimate expenditure of $50,000,000 or 8100,000,000. This year, when we most need the work, we have the smallest expenditure on public works that has been made since I have been a member of this house. I think government activity in connection with public works shall be speeded up whenever there is evidence of a slackening of employment in private industry. We should use our own national credit to finance these undertakings instead of borrowing from our financial houses at ruinous rates of interest, such as the provinces and the Dominion have been forced to pay recently. Our national wealth is estimated at some 830,000,000,000, so it is absurd for us to talk of this dominion going bankrupt or running short of credit. There is still plenty of real credit on which to draw, so let us use our own credit, put our people to work and restore the confidence of the people in our own institutions.

speechtext:
We cannot sell them because there is no money with which to buy them, and you will not get any improvement in business until you put money into the hands of the purchasers. The great body of purchasers in Canada to-day have lost their purchasing power. The farmers represent from 45 per cent to 47 per cent of our population, and their purchasing power has been more than cut in half. Thousands of people who have been working for wages have lost their jobs; their purchasing power has been cut by 80 per cent, and now I suppose the purchasing power of the civil servants has been cut by 10 per cent. Thousands of people have had their incomes reduced, and all these things tend to decrease purchasing power. When you decrease the purchasing power of these people our factories must lay off many workers, who in turn become unemployed and lose their purchasing power. It is the most vicious circle that can be imagined, and the only way to get out of that circle is to put money in circulation. This can be done only by putting people to work, because only when they work do they produce something which gives value to money.
I was told to-day by a man who for years has been a student of economics, and who I believe is a graduate in economics of one of our universities, that a thirty per cent rise in commodity price levels would reduce the burden of debt of the municipalities, the provinces and the dominion by S75,000.000. Surely that is worth while. You can add to that the increase in revenue from taxation, because the amount of taxes received depends upon the amount of trade carried on. You can also add the reduced expenditure by all our governments for unemployment relief, as well as the increase in trade which would be brought about by increasing the income of our farmers and by increasing the employment of our artisans and labourers. In addition there would be the increased spending power which they would have, and added to that there would be the very distinct benefit, at least so far as the Prime Minister is concerned, that an adverse trade balance, if any, would be corrected.
I have taken a -little longer on this question than I had- intended, but before I sit down I would like to make some reference to the proposal which I understood the minister to

say had 'been made to the provinces, that the federal and provincial governments should cooperate to place some of the unemployed on farms in Canada. In that connection I would like to quote from a little book which recently came to my notice, entitled The Cause and Cure of Unemployment. The author is John S. Lennox, an engineer in the United States who graduated from Queen's university some years ago. It is rather significant that to-day so many of our engineers have taken to the study of economics, and some of them have put in writing their opinions as to the cause and cure of unemployment. I -may say very frankly that if we would charge some of our eminent Canadian engineers with the study of the financial question, it would not take them very long to evolve a better financial system than- we are trying to work under at the present time. In regard to the farm problem Mr. Lennox says:
There has been no general recognition of the fact that farming is the only business in which a man can procure food and shelter when receiving no wages. Until the tax collector and the landlord can no longer be put off a farmer can stay in business. The lower selling prices go, the more produce he must market, even though he is selling at a loss. The hired man will work for his board and enough to keep him in boots and overalls. Truly, agriculture is the great unemployment sponge.
With reference to the remark that the hired man will work for his board and enough to keep him in boots and overalls, I might relate to this house a sentence or two from a letter which I received from an Alberta farmer last summer. I must remind the house that the letter was written last August when the weather was very hot. With reference to the statement Iby one of our leading statesmen that he was not afraid of the farmer starving, this man stated in his 'letter, "Of course the farmers will not starve; we still have milk and potatoes, but the clothes we bought in more prosperous years soon will be worn out, and we may have to resort to rhubarb leaves." There is much more in this booklet I should like to read to the committee, but I do not think I should take the time.
In conclusion I should like to say to the Minister of Labour that if the dominion and provincial governments are justified in cooperating to place unemployed people on farms, surely there is every justification for these two governments cooperating to keep the tax collector and the mortgage companies from putting farmers off the land. That is what is going to happen unless something is done to forestall that action. What is the sense of allowing these men to be forced off their farms? They will simply go to the cities to 
take the places of the unemployed whom the two governments are now endeavouring to take from the cities and place on the land. I do suggest to the minister that this is one of the most necessary things for agriculture to-day; otherwise some farmers are going to become charges upon the country. They will have to drift into the cities and receive direct unemployment relief.

I cannot understand the mentality of a man who will strenuously oppose a ten per cent reduction in salaries and wages, and in the same breath advocate a policy of monetary inflation the immediate effect of which would be to cut in half all salaries and all wages.
I can agree with my hon .friend this far, that the present depression will not lift until we have discovered the fundamental causes and removed them. I agree with him there, but the immediate problem before the committee to-night is what to do with our unemployed who do not know where to sleep, who do not know where their next meal is coming from, and who do not know where they are going to get clothes with which to protect themselves and their children from the weather. These people cannot wait while our economists, our statesmen and our politicians debate as to what is the cause of the trouble, and try to agree on a remedy. They must have action and immediate action. I cannot support the policy of creating great public works at the present time out of the public treasury for the purpose of giving people employment. Take, for instance, the suggestion made to-night of a trans-Canada highway. The principal abjection I see to it is this. If we were to construct such a highway and by that means give employment to so many thousands of people while it was in course of construction, once it was finished, after the depression had lifted, we should find ourselves saddled in *perpetuity with the expense of maintaining it, which we know from experience would run *into millions and millions every year. We cannot afford any such undertaking.
There is a plan being operated at the present time to a limited degree in the province of Saskatchewan which I would commend to the minister. I do not know who originated it, but whoever did deserves, I believe, some credit. The plan is simplicity itself. It proposes to put men who are free to go, mostly single men, on farms, the government paying each man five dollars a month and paying the farmer five dollars a month to keep him. He is supported then in food, shelter and clothing at a total cost to the government of ten dollars a month. I do not think it can

be done cheaper in any other way. There must be in Canada hundreds of thousands of farmers who would like to make improvements on their farms, farmers who no doubt would have liked to do so years ago, but who could never afford it because they could not pay the necessary wages to hire men for the purpose. Now is an opportunity for these men to get cheap help with which to make these improvements. I believe that we could give employment to 100,000 men in this way, at a total cost to the government of not more than ten dollars per month per man, and when the work was done the government would not be saddled with enormous expense such as would be involved in any structure built up under a relief measure. As I say, I do not know who originated the scheme, and it is working only to a limited extent, but I believe it is capable of vast expansion and I commend it to the minister.

speechtext:
The debate has got away
from the actual resolution before the house. The resolution proposes steps to deal directly with the distress due to unemployment, but we seem to have got into a general academic discussion with regard to the original causes of the present situation, which is a matter that has been discussed at considerable length already in this house. The minister was courteous enough a few days ago to say that he would welcome any suggestions made by members, and while he would not, of course, guarantee to adopt them, he intimated that he would consider them before introducing the bill. That seems to me a very reasonable suggestion, and it is much more advisable than simply bringing in a bill and leaving us to criticize it without any hope of having any changes made in its provisions. I should like to take advantage for a very few minutes of that offer to mention one or two suggestions, which I hope will be found practical, dealing directly with the subject under discussion.
I am glad to see that the Minister of Public Works is here. I would call his attention to the statement made by the Prime Minister the other day, very plainly, that there was to be no federal relief work as such done this year. Now the Minister of Public Works will recall that last year his estimates were very badly smashed, so much so as to be almost unrecognizable so far as carrying out any necessary maintenance of public works was concerned. The situation was remedied when we came to unemployment relief by his doing the necessary maintenance works under the provisions of the relief fund. In some
ways it was a good idea; at any rate it furnished some work for unemployed people, and it also provided the necessary maintenance, failure to provide which would have been very bad policy indeed on the part of the department. We find this year that the situation is very much the same, only worse. The minister has practically cut his estimates to the disappearing point, possibly with the same idea in view, that he will get the necessary expenditures made out of the unemployment relief fund. A glance at the estimates will show that he has made hardly any provision for the necessary work.
This is not the place or the time to point out to the minister what very bad policy, a policy of penny wise and pound foolish, it is to neglect the maintenance of wharves and floats which have only a short life anyhow; for if maintenance is not carried on year by year it means double expense in the future to make repairs. In the meantime these public conveniences are standing idle during a considerable period of their very short life, hampering industrial development and inconveniencing the public. As the minister has made the cut even worse this year than it was last year, I want to point out to him that he is now confronted with the situation that no relief will accrue to him from the unemployment relief fund. There is to be no federal relief work undertaken, so I suggest to him with all deference that it is very much up to him to take steps to see that in the supplementary estimates arrangements will be made to carry out the most necessary public works required.
As regards other suggestions, we understand now that we are committed to a policy of direct relief only. So far as British Columbia is concerned, 1 have no doubt that the government will make or has made representations, and judging from the press I gather that its wishes are opposite to that. In that province the government apparently wish public relief works continued on various grounds-that it will provide work, it will not destroy the morale of the men, and some return will be made for the money spent. So far as the cities are concerned, the same view is held. Certainly the smaller cities will be against the policy of direct relief only. Not only is it better for men to do some work for the relief they are given, but the small cities have plenty of work to do and naturally they want some return for their money. If we are going to go in for direct relief, however, and whether we do or not, I want to point out to the minister that we shall have to make greater provision to help the cities. They are almost at the end of their financial resources. They have
